## Q1
A problem of size n requires n² bit operations. What is the largest instance that can be solved in one second if each bit operation takes 10⁻⁹ second?

## Q1 - Options
(A) 10⁹
(B) 3.16 × 10⁴
(C) 3.96 × 10⁷
(D) 2 × 10⁹

## Q1 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Time Complexity, Asymptotic Notation & Recurrences
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2026 (22 Jun, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q48

One second permits 10⁹ operations. Solving n² = 10⁹ gives n = √10⁹ ≈ 3.16 × 10⁴. The larger choices confuse the operation budget with the square root of that budget.

## Q2
If f(n) = θ(g(n)) and g(n) = O(h(n)), which statement is true?

## Q2 - Options
(A) f(n) = O(h(n))
(B) f(n) = θ(h(n))
(C) h(n) = O(f(n))
(D) h(n) = θ(f(n))

## Q2 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Time Complexity, Asymptotic Notation & Recurrences
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2026 (22 Jun, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q79

f(n) = θ(g(n)) implies f(n) = O(g(n)). Combining this with g(n) = O(h(n)) and transitivity of big-O gives f(n) = O(h(n)). The information does not establish a reverse bound, so the theta claims need not hold.

## Q3
Which of the following is the correct order of increasing time complexity of the given algorithms?<br>
A. Tower of Hanoi with n disks<br>
B. Binary search given n sorted numbers<br>
C. Heap sort given n numbers, worst case<br>
D. Addition of two n × n matrices

## Q3 - Options
(A) B, C, D, A
(B) A, B, C, D
(C) D, C, B, A
(D) C, A, D, B

## Q3 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Time Complexity, Asymptotic Notation & Recurrences
**Source:** UGC NET Jan 2026 (2 Jan, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q50

Each algorithm has a standard, well-known time complexity.

- **Binary search on n sorted numbers** — O(log n).
- **Heap sort, worst case** — O(n log n).
- **Addition of two n × n matrices** — O(n²), since every one of the n² entries needs one addition.
- **Tower of Hanoi with n disks** — O(2ⁿ), since the number of moves doubles with each additional disk.

Ordering these by growth rate from smallest to largest gives log n &lt; n log n &lt; n² &lt; 2ⁿ, so the increasing order is Binary search, Heap sort, Matrix addition, Tower of Hanoi — that is, B, C, D, A.

## Q4
Which of the following is the correct solution of the given recurrence relation?

T(n) = 3T(n/4) + n log n

## Q4 - Options
(A) θ(n log n)
(B) θ(n² log n)
(C) θ(n(log n)²)
(D) θ(n log log n)

## Q4 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Time Complexity, Asymptotic Notation & Recurrences
**Source:** UGC NET Jan 2026 (2 Jan, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q53

The Master theorem applies directly to T(n) = 3T(n/4) + n log n, with a = 3, b = 4 and f(n) = n log n.

Compare f(n) against n^(log_b a): log_4 3 ≈ 0.7925, so n^(log_4 3) ≈ n^0.7925.

Since n log n grows polynomially faster than n^0.7925 for large n, this falls under Master theorem Case 3.

Case 3 also needs the regularity condition a·f(n/b) ≤ c·f(n) for some c &lt; 1. Checking it: 3·(n/4)log(n/4) = 0.75·n·log(n/4), which stays below 0.75·n log n for large n, so the condition holds.

Under Case 3, T(n) = Θ(f(n)) = Θ(n log n).

## Q10
Match List I with List II on Fibonacci computation running times.

| List I | List II |
|---|---|
| A. The running time of the straightforward recursive method to compute the nth Fibonacci number Fn | I. O(n²) |
| B. The running time to compute Fn using memoization | II. O(lg n) |
| C. The running time to compute a Fibonacci number Fn using only integer addition and multiplication | III. O(n) |
| D. The running time to determine an optimal bitonic tour | IV. Θ(φⁿ) |

List I to List II matching for Fibonacci computation and bitonic tour running times

## Q10 - Options
(A) A-I, B-III, C-IV, D-II
(B) A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I
(C) A-I, B-II, C-IV, D-III
(D) A-IV, B-II, C-III, D-I

## Q10 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Time Complexity, Asymptotic Notation & Recurrences
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q11

Each item names a distinct, well-known algorithmic running time from the analysis of Fibonacci computation and tour optimization.

A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I

- The naive recursive Fibonacci algorithm branches into two calls at every step without reusing results, giving an exponential running time of Θ(φⁿ), where φ is the golden ratio.
- Memoization stores each Fibonacci value the first time it is computed, so computing Fn takes only O(n) time since each of the n subproblems is solved once.
- Computing Fn using only integer addition and multiplication refers to the matrix-power or fast-doubling method, which needs only O(lg n) multiplications through repeated squaring.
- Finding an optimal bitonic tour is solved with a dynamic programming table over pairs of endpoints, which runs in O(n²) time.

## Q11
Let f(n) and g(n) be asymptotically positive functions.

Statement I: f(n) = O(g(n)) ⇒ g(n) = Ω(f(n))<br>
Statement II: f(n) = O(g(n)) ⇒ lg(f(n)) = O(lg(g(n))), where lg(g(n)) ≥ 1 and f(n) ≥ 1 for all sufficiently large n.

## Q11 - Options
(A) Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
(B) Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
(C) Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
(D) Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

## Q11 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Time Complexity, Asymptotic Notation & Recurrences
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q56

Statement I restates the direct duality between Big-O and Big-Omega: if f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all sufficiently large n (f = O(g)), then equivalently g(n) ≥ (1/c)·f(n) for the same n, which is exactly the definition of g(n) = Ω(f(n)). This equivalence holds unconditionally for asymptotically positive functions, so Statement I is correct.

Statement II follows by taking logarithms of the same inequality. From f(n) ≤ c·g(n), taking lg of both sides gives lg f(n) ≤ lg c + lg g(n). Since the statement guarantees lg g(n) ≥ 1 for large n, the constant term can be absorbed as (lg c + 1)·lg g(n) ≥ lg c + lg g(n), giving lg f(n) ≤ (lg c + 1)·lg g(n) — exactly the definition of lg f(n) = O(lg g(n)). So Statement II is also correct.

- **A. Both Statement I and Statement II are correct** — correct, both follow directly from the definitions of O and Ω plus one logarithm substitution.
- **B. Both incorrect** — contradicts the direct O/Ω duality in Statement I.
- **C. Statement I correct but Statement II incorrect** — Statement II also holds once the stated conditions (lg g(n) ≥ 1, f(n) ≥ 1) are applied.
- **D. Statement I incorrect but Statement II correct** — Statement I is a basic, unconditional definitional duality and is not incorrect.

## Q12
Statement I: If f and g are two functions and f = O(g) but g is not o(f), we say that the growth rate of g is smaller than that of f<br>
Statement II: The class of all decision problems decided by a Turing Machine in exponential time, that is O(2^k) where k is a constant, is called EXP

Which one of the following is correct in the light of the above statements?

## Q12 - Options
(A) Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
(B) Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
(C) Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
(D) Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct

## Q12 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Time Complexity, Asymptotic Notation & Recurrences
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q89

Statement I is incorrect. f = O(g) only says f does not grow faster than g. Adding that g is not o(f) rules out g being strictly slower than f, and together these two facts mean f and g grow at the same rate, f = Θ(g), not that g grows slower than f. For example, f(n) = g(n) = n satisfies f = O(g) and g is not o(f), yet the two functions have identical growth, contradicting the statement's claim that g's growth rate is smaller.

Statement II is correct. A decision problem is in the complexity class EXP (EXPTIME) exactly when some deterministic Turing machine decides it in exponential time, bounded by 2 raised to a polynomial in the input size for some constant exponent. This is the standard definition of the exponential-time class.

Since Statement I is incorrect and Statement II is correct, the matching option is the one stating exactly that.

## Q13
Let 'n' denote a positive integer. Suppose a function F is defined as

f(n) = 0, n = 1 f(n) = f(⌊n/2⌋) + 1, n &gt; 1

What is f(25)? and what does this function find?

## Q13 - Options
(A) 4, ⌊log₂ n⌋
(B) 14, ⌊log₂ n⌋
(C) 4, ⌊n/2⌋
(D) 14, ⌊n/2⌋

## Q13 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Time Complexity, Asymptotic Notation & Recurrences
**Source:** UGC NET Mar 2023 (11 Mar, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q26

Unroll the recursion by repeatedly halving 25 and flooring, because each call adds exactly 1 to the result.

f(25) = f(12) + 1 f(12) = f(6) + 1 f(6) = f(3) + 1 f(3) = f(1) + 1 = 0 + 1 = 1

Substituting back gives f(6) = 2, f(12) = 3, and f(25) = 4.

Each call halves n, so f(n) counts how many times n can be halved before reaching 1, which is exactly ⌊log₂ n⌋. Since 2^4 = 16 ≤ 25 &lt; 32 = 2^5, ⌊log₂ 25⌋ = 4, matching the computed value.

## Q14
Assume that f(n) and g(n) are asymptotically positive. Which of the following is correct?

## Q14 - Options
(A) f(n)=O(g(n)) and g(n)=O(h(n)) ⇒ f(n)=ω(h(n))
(B) f(n)=Ω(g(n)) and g(n)=Ω(h(n)) ⇒ f(n)=O(h(n))
(C) f(n)=o(g(n)) and g(n)=o(h(n)) ⇒ f(n)=o(h(n))
(D) f(n)=ω(g(n)) and g(n)=ω(h(n)) ⇒ f(n)=Ω(h(n))

## Q14 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Time Complexity, Asymptotic Notation & Recurrences
**Source:** UGC NET Oct 2022 (8 Oct, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q42

Little-o is transitive in the exact sense stated. If f(n) = o(g(n)) and g(n) = o(h(n)), then f(n) grows strictly slower than g(n), which in turn grows strictly slower than h(n), so f(n) must also grow strictly slower than h(n), giving f(n) = o(h(n)).

- **A. O∘O ⇒ ω** — wrong direction. Composing two upper-bound (O) relations should yield another upper bound O(h(n)), not the strict lower-bound claim ω(h(n)).
- **B. Ω∘Ω ⇒ O** — wrong direction. Composing two lower-bound (Ω) relations should yield another lower bound Ω(h(n)), not the opposite upper-bound claim O(h(n)).
- **C. o∘o ⇒ o** — correct. This matches the standard transitive closure of the strict little-o relation.
- **D. ω∘ω ⇒ Ω** — imprecise. Composing two strict lower-bound (ω) relations should yield the matching strict bound ω(h(n)), not the weaker Ω(h(n)) claim, so this does not state the standard identity being tested.

## Q15
The solution of the recurrence relation T(n) = 3T(n/4) + n lg n is

## Q15 - Options
(A) θ(n² lg n)
(B) θ(n lg n)
(C) θ(n lg n)²
(D) θ(n lg lg n)

## Q15 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Time Complexity, Asymptotic Notation & Recurrences
**Source:** UGC NET Oct 2022 (8 Oct, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q43

Apply the master theorem with a = 3, b = 4, and f(n) = n lg n.

n^(log_b a) = n^(log₄3) ≈ n^0.792

Since f(n) = n lg n grows polynomially faster than n^0.792 (the exponent 1 already exceeds 0.792, so the extra lg n factor only helps), this falls under Master Theorem Case 3, and the regularity condition a·f(n/b) ≤ c·f(n) holds for a suitable c &lt; 1.

So T(n) = θ(f(n)) = θ(n lg n).

## Q16
Match each algorithm with its running-time complexity.

| Algorithm | Complexity |
|---|---|
| A. Breadth First Search | II. O(V+E) |
| B. Rabin-Karp Algorithm | III. θ((n−m+1)m) |
| C. Depth-First Search | I. θ(V+E) |
| D. Heap sort (worst case) | V. O(n lg n) |
| E. Quick sort (worst case) | IV. O(n²) |

## Q16 - Options
(A) (A)-(III), (B)-(II), (C)-(I), (D)-(IV), (E)-(V)
(B) (A)-(II), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(IV), (E)-(V)
(C) (A)-(II), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(V), (E)-(IV)
(D) (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(II), (D)-(IV), (E)-(V)

## Q16 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Time Complexity, Asymptotic Notation & Recurrences
**Source:** UGC NET Oct 2022 (8 Oct, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q75

Breadth-first search and depth-first search both run in O(V+E) (equivalently θ(V+E)) time on an adjacency-list graph.<br>
Rabin-Karp string matching has worst-case complexity θ((n−m+1)m).<br>
Heap sort runs in O(n lg n) in every case, including the worst case, since it always maintains a balanced heap.<br>
Quick sort's worst case is O(n²), which happens when the pivot repeatedly gives the most unbalanced possible split.

The key distinguishing check here is D and E. Heap sort's worst case is never quadratic, and quick sort's worst case is never O(n lg n), so D must be O(n lg n) and E must be O(n²), which only option C gets right.

## Q21
Give asymptotic upper and lower bound for T(n) given below. Assume T(n) is constant for n ≤ 2.

T(n) = 4T(√n) + lg²n

## Q21 - Options
(A) T(n) = θ(lg(lg²n) lg n)
(B) T(n) = θ(lg²n lg n)
(C) T(n) = θ(lg²n lg lg n)
(D) T(n) = θ(lg(lg n) lg n)

## Q21 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Time Complexity, Asymptotic Notation & Recurrences
**Source:** UGC NET Dec 2019 (4 Dec, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q17

Solve by substitution of variable:<br>
Let n = 2ᵐ, so m = lg n and √n = 2^(m/2).

The recurrence becomes:<br>
T(2ᵐ) = 4T(2^(m/2)) + m²

Define S(m) = T(2ᵐ):<br>
S(m) = 4S(m/2) + m²

Apply the Master Theorem to S(m) = 4S(m/2) + m²:

- a = 4, b = 2
- m^(log_b a) = m^(log₂ 4) = m²
- f(m) = m² = θ(m^(log_b a))

This falls into Case 2 of the Master Theorem:<br>
S(m) = θ(m² lg m)

Substitute back m = lg n:<br>
T(n) = θ((lg n)² lg(lg n)) = θ(lg²n lg lg n)

## Q22
Consider the following pseudo-code fragment in which an invariant for the loop is "m\*x^k = p^n and k ≥ 0" (here, p and n are integer variables that have been initialized):

```
/* Pre-conditions: p ≥ 1 ∧ n ≥ 0 */
/* Assume that overflow never occurs */
int x = p; int k = n; int m = 1;
while (k <> 0) {
  if (k is odd) then m = m*x;
  x = x*x;
  k = [k/2]; /* floor(k/2) */
}
```

Which of the following must be true at the end of the while loop?

## Q22 - Options
(A) x = p^n
(B) m = p^n
(C) p = x^n
(D) p = m^n

## Q22 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Time Complexity, Asymptotic Notation & Recurrences
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2019 (24 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q77

Analyzing the loop termination condition using the established invariant:

The given loop invariant is:<br>
m \* x^k = p^n and k &gt;= 0.

The while loop terminates when the loop guard fails (k = 0).<br>
Substituting k = 0 into the invariant equation:<br>
m \* x^0 = p^n<br>
Since x^0 = 1, this simplifies directly to:<br>
m \* 1 = p^n m = p^n.

Thus, m = p^n must hold upon loop completion.

(Note : a loop invariant for a while statement is an assertion that is true each time the guard is evaluated during the execution of the while statement).

## Q23 - Options
(A) p = 2^(k+1) – 1 and 0 ≤ k &lt; m
(B) p = 2^k – 1 and 0 ≤ k &lt; m
(C) p = 2^k – 1 and 0 ≤ k ≤ m
(D) p = 2^(k+1) – 1 and 0 ≤ k ≤ m

## Q23 - Hint
**Answer:** C
**Topic:** Time Complexity, Asymptotic Notation & Recurrences
**Source:** UGC NET Dec 2018 (20 Dec, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q13

The loop invariant must hold each time the while guard is tested, including upon initial entry and upon final loop termination when k = m.

- At initialization (k = 0), p = 0, which satisfies 2^0 - 1 = 0.
- After k iterations, p accumulates 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + 2^(k-1) = 2^k - 1.
- During loop execution, the guard (k &lt; m) is evaluated for k = 0, 1, ..., m.
- Upon loop termination, k reaches m, making k &lt;= m necessary to describe the valid range of k at every evaluation of the guard.
- Therefore, the invariant is p = 2^k - 1 and 0 &lt;= k &lt;= m (Option C).

## Q24
The solution of recurrence relation :

T(n) = 2T (√n) + lg (n)

is :

## Q24 - Options
(A) O(lg (n) lg(lg (n)))
(B) O(n lg (n))
(C) O(lg (n))
(D) O(lg (n) lg (n))

## Q24 - Hint
**Answer:** A
**Topic:** Time Complexity, Asymptotic Notation & Recurrences
**Source:** UGC NET Dec 2018 (20 Dec, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q33

Transforming the domain with variable substitution solves the square-root recurrence relation.

Let n = 2^m, which implies m = lg n and √n = 2^(m/2).<br>
Substituting into the recurrence:<br>
T(2^m) = 2T(2^(m/2)) + m.

Define S(m) = T(2^m):<br>
S(m) = 2 S(m/2) + m.

Applying the Master Theorem to S(m) = 2 S(m/2) + m:<br>
a = 2, b = 2, and f(m) = m = m^(log_2 2) = m^1.<br>
This matches Case 2 of the Master Theorem:<br>
S(m) = Theta(m lg m).

Substituting back m = lg n:<br>
T(n) = Theta(lg n \* lg(lg n)) = O(lg (n) lg(lg (n))).

- Therefore, Option A is the exact asymptotic solution.
